(CNN) -- Around 200 new species of frogs have been found in Madagascar, one of the world's biodiversity hotspots. A study has found nearly 200 new species of frogs in Madagascar. A study identified between 129 and 221 new species of frogs on the island. The Spanish Scientific Research Council (CSIC), who carried out the study, believe the find could practically double the number of amphibians known in the world if the results are extrapolated at a global scale. The study, published in the journal "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA," suggests that the number of amphibian species in Madagascar has been significantly underestimated. "The diversity of species in Madagascar is far from being known and there is still a lot of scientific research to be done. Our data suggest that the number of new species of amphibians not only has been underestimated but it is spatially widespread, even in well studied areas," said Professor David R. Vieites, CSIC researcher to the press at the Spanish National Natural Sciences Museum in Madrid. "For example, two of the most visited and studied national parks, Ranomafana and Mantadía/Analamazaotra, harbor 31 and 10 new species respectively." Dr. Frank Glaw, curator of herpetology at the Zoologische Staatssammlung from Munich was part of the research team: "During the past 15 years, we discovered and described over 100 new frog species from Madagascar, which led us to believe that our species inventory is almost complete. But as our new surveys show, there are many more species than we suspected," he said in a press statement. The paper suggests that the total biodiversity on the island could be much higher in other species as well, so the actual destruction of natural habitats may be affecting more animals than previously thought. This has important consequences for conservation planning, as the rate of destruction of rainforests in Madagascar has been one of the highest in the planet, with more than 80 percent of the historic surface of rainforest already lost, according to the study's authors. Almost a quarter of the new species discovered have not been found yet in protected areas, but the unstable political situation in Madagascar has also been cited as hampering conservation efforts. "Although a lot of reserves and national parks have been created in Madagascar during the last decade, the actual situation of politic instability is allowing the cut of the forest within national parks, generating a lot of uncertainty about the future of the planned network of protected areas", said Vieites. Madagascar is the fourth largest island in the world and one of the most biodiverse areas globally, with a high degree of endemic species. "To get an idea of its biodiversity --while in the Iberian Peninsula [there] are about 30 species of amphibians and in Germany about 20, in a single locality in Madagascar we can find around 100 species of frogs," said Vieites. Dr. Miguel Vences, professor at the Technical University of Braunschweig, Germany, who was also part of the study team, and believes that a century of new species discovery is just beginning: "People think that we know which plant and animal species live on this planet. But the majority of life forms on Earth is still awaiting scientific recognition."

**By** Jacqui Palumbo, CNN  
**Updated** 4:12 PM EDT, Thursday, October 24, 2024

**(CNN) —** In a monumental discovery that highlights both the breathtaking richness and the extreme fragility of Earth’s ecosystems, an international team of scientists has identified nearly 200 new species of frogs on the island nation of Madagascar. 

The finding, published in a comprehensive study following years of extensive fieldwork and genetic analysis, effectively doubles the known number of amphibian species inhabiting the Indian Ocean island.

Research teams trekking through Madagascar’s dense rainforests, arid canyons, and high-altitude mountains uncovered a staggering array of previously unrecorded frogs. The new species range from tiny, leaf-litter dwellers smaller than a human fingernail to vibrant, tree-dwelling amphibians boasting striking shades of neon green and burnt orange.

"Madagascar was already known as a biodiversity hotspot, but these results show we have barely scratched the surface," said Dr. Mark Scherz, Curator of Herpetology at the Natural History Museum of Denmark and one of the lead authors of the research. "To find this many new species in one swoop is staggering. It’s like discovering an entirely new chapter in the book of life."

### A hidden world revealed by DNA

For centuries, many of these species remained hidden in plain sight. Many of the newly identified frogs are what scientists call "cryptic species"—animals that look almost identical to the naked eye but possess entirely distinct genetic profiles and unique mating calls. 

To untangle the complex web of species, the research team combined traditional field observation with advanced DNA sequencing and acoustic analysis. By recording the distinctive nocturnal calls of the frogs and analyzing their tissue samples, scientists confirmed that populations once thought to be a single species were actually dozens of distinct evolutionary lineages.

"You can look at two frogs and swear they are identical," Scherz told CNN. "But then you listen to their calls, look at their DNA, and realize they’ve been evolving separately for millions of years."

### A paradise under siege

Madagascar, which broke away from the Indian subcontinent roughly 88 million years ago, is an evolutionary laboratory. More than 90% of its wildlife—including its famous lemurs and chameleons—is endemic, meaning it is found nowhere else on Earth.

However, the thrill of the discovery is heavily tempered by the reality of Madagascar’s environmental crisis.

Because many of the newly discovered frog species are micro-endemics—living only within a single valley or on a specific mountain peak—even localized deforestation could instantly wipe an entire species off the planet.

"The tragedy is that many of these species may be pushed to extinction before we even finish naming them," said Dr. Harison Randrianto, a Malagasy conservation specialist who contributed to the study. "Amphibians are the clear warning system for an ecosystem's health. When they start disappearing, it means the whole system is collapsing."

Climate change presents another looming threat. As temperatures rise and weather patterns shift, frogs living at high altitudes have nowhere higher to go to escape the heat. 

### A call for urgent protection

Scientists hope this massive discovery will push international conservation organizations and the Malagasy government to expand protected areas across the island. 

The researchers emphasized that local community involvement is critical. Conservation programs that offer sustainable livelihoods to local residents—such as eco-tourism and sustainable farming—are essential to stopping the destruction of the frogs' habitat.

"This discovery isn't just a triumph for science; it's a call to action," Randrianto said. "We have been handed a map to a hidden treasure trove of nature. Now, the world has to help us protect it."

To penetrate this evolutionary camouflage, the research team—led by Dr. David R. The results were staggering. The study revealed that Madagascar harbors between 129 and 221 previously unknown, candidate amphibian species, boosting the island’s total frog species richness from roughly 244 to well over 460.

"The sheer scale of this hidden diversity was breathtaking," said **Dr. David R. Vieites**, lead author of the CSIC study. "We knew there were undiscovered frogs in Madagascar, but our genomic data showed that we had barely scratched the surface. We are not just talking about finding a few isolated species; we are looking at entire evolutionary lineages that were completely invisible to us using traditional techniques."

### **Deciphering the Whispers of the Rainforest**

A key driver behind these discoveries was the field recording of frog calls. In the dense foliage of eastern rainforests like Masoala and Ranomafana, physical sightings are rare, but acoustic signatures are unmistakable.

"Two frogs might appear completely identical under a microscope, but their genetics and their voice tell a vastly different story," explained **Dr. Frank Glaw**, a renowned herpetologist at the Bavarian State Collection of Zoology (ZSM) and co-author of the study. "A male frog’s call is a species-specific fingerprint designed to attract mates of the exact same lineage. By listening to the rainforest at night, we realized that what we thought was a single, widespread species was actually a complex cluster of five or six distinct species, each restricted to its own tiny patch of mountain or valley."

This phenomenon—known as micro-endemism—means many of these newly uncovered species occupy extremely narrow geographic ranges, sometimes limited to a single mountain ridge or isolated forest fragment.

### **A Race Against Habitat Loss**

While the scientific implications of the study are profound, its conservation implications are terrifying. Because these species live in such restricted areas, even localized habitat destruction can push an entire lineage into extinction overnight.

The PNAS paper emphasizes that current protected area maps were drawn without knowledge of these hidden micro-endemic hotspots, leaving vast swathes of irreplaceable biodiversity entirely vulnerable.

If a single hillside is cleared for farmland, an entire species that science just discovered yesterday could be wiped off the face of the planet tomorrow."

The ecological crisis in Madagascar is deeply entangled with its socio-political landscape. "Conservation cannot exist in a vacuum," said **Miguel Vences**. "When a country experiences severe political instability, the immediate casualty—after human security—is the environment.
